title: Library of carbon nanotube junctions: data-driven insights into structure-magnetotransport relationships
authors: Juan Alberto Canché-Martín, Teresa Kulka, Jacek A. Majewski, Irina V. Lebedeva, Maciej Marchwiany, Karolina Z. Milowska
abstract: Electronic transport in carbon nanotube (CNT) assemblies is controlled by a heterogeneous population of CNT--CNT junctions, yet most microscopic studies consider only a few representative systems. Here, we construct a library of 146 single-walled carbon nanotube (SWCNT)--SWCNT junctions spanning broad structural and electronic diversity and analyse their magnetotransport using an automated workflow combining molecular dynamics, tight-binding theory, Peierls magnetic coupling, and non-equilibrium Green's functions.The resulting transport data are subsequently analysed using machine-learning methods. Two complementary transport descriptors reveal distinct structure--transport hierarchies. The averaged first transmission-step value is governed primarily by the mean chiral angle of the two nanotubes forming a junction, whereas the energy gap of the junction depends predominantly on the metallic or semiconducting character of the constituent CNTs. Temperature generally suppresses the averaged transmission while reducing the extracted gap, whereas a perpendicular magnetic field affects transmission much more strongly than the gap. Signatures of interference-driven transport remain visible even at $300~\mathrm{K}$. Notably, semiconducting--semiconducting junctions retain the largest gaps but, once shifted into their conducting regime, can exhibit transmission comparable to or exceeding that of metallic junctions. These results establish statistically robust junction-level trends that can inform future network-scale models of CNT assemblies.
summary: This work constructs a large library of carbon nanotube junctions and uses advanced computational methods to map out their magnetotransport behavior. It reveals that junction conductance is sensitive to the junction's average chiral angle, while the energy gap is dictated by the electronic nature (metallic vs. semiconducting) of the connected tubes. These findings establish crucial, statistically robust rules for designing CNT-based electronic networks.
main_problem: The study investigates how the specific structure of individual carbon nanotube (CNT) junctions dictates their magnetotransport properties across a diverse population of junctions.
main_result: The average transmission step is primarily governed by the mean chiral angle, while the junction energy gap depends predominantly on the metallic or semiconducting nature of the constituent CNTs.
method: The authors employed an automated, high-throughput workflow combining molecular dynamics, tight-binding theory, Peierls magnetic coupling, and non-equilibrium Green's functions, followed by machine-learning analysis.
model_or_system: The system consists of single-walled carbon nanotube (SWCNT)–SWCNT junctions, with a library of 146 junctions constructed spanning various structural and electronic types. The calculations utilize an empirical tight-binding model incorporating curvature and inter-nanotube coupling.
key_observables: Averaged first transmission-step value, junction energy gap, and transport characteristics as a function of temperature and perpendicular magnetic field.
important_parameters: Mean chiral angle, metallic/semiconducting character of constituent CNTs, temperature (up to 300 K), and perpendicular magnetic field strength.
main_assumptions: The analysis uses an empirical tight-binding model and makes approximations regarding orbital directions (radial approximation) and hopping integrals.
figures_summary: Figures summarize the workflow, showing how transport properties (transmission spectra and band gaps) are calculated and analyzed across varying magnetic fields, temperatures, and junction metallicities.
paper_structure: The paper first details the construction of the diverse junction library and the complex computational workflow. It then presents the analysis of key transport descriptors, establishing distinct structure-transport hierarchies, and concludes by providing statistically robust trends for network-scale modeling.
why_interesting: The detailed, first-principles study of quantum transport in nanoscale junctions, particularly the separation of descriptors governing conductance versus gap size, provides valuable insights into mesoscopic physics relevant to quantum devices.
